sections.html:
Norfolk is an independent city in the southeastern corner of Virginia, where the Elizabeth River meets the Chesapeake Bay. No county sits above it, so the city handles its own assessments, tax billing and zoning. Of its 96.41 square miles, 53.28 are land and 43.13 are water, and the average elevation is about 6.9 feet. The 2020 census counted 238,005 residents, and the 2025 estimate is 231,013.

That low, watery footprint explains most of what buyers worry about here. Flood zone, drainage and the age of the structure come up in nearly every Norfolk conversation.

sections.h2: Neighborhoods and what buyers ask about
sections.html:
Norfolk has dozens of named neighborhoods, and house age and style change from one to the next.

  • Freemason and West Freemason: historic downtown neighborhoods with some of the oldest buildings in the city.
  • Berkley: a former separate city across the Elizabeth River, annexed in 1906.
  • Willoughby Spit and Ocean View: bay-front areas.
  • Ghent, Colonial Place, Larchmont, North Shore, Edgewater and Lafayette Shores: popular residential areas.
  • Downtown, Ghent and Fairmount Park: areas reshaped by revitalization.

A pre-war rowhouse in Ghent, a bayside house in Ocean View and a mid-century home in Larchmont raise different repair and flood questions. A walk-through usually comes before any price.

Flooding is the main building concern in Norfolk. The city is low, nearly surrounded by water and slowly subsiding, and some areas already flood at high tide. Heavy rain and wind are most likely from mid-August through September. Summers are warm and humid, and winters are mild.

The city explains its flood rules on the Flood Zones page. FEMA's Flood Insurance Rate Map sets the zones, and the city enforces them through Article 3.9.7 of its zoning ordinance and the Virginia Uniform Statewide Building Code. The zones break down this way:

  • X: outside the 0.2% annual chance flood area, the least likely to flood.
  • X shaded: 0.2% annual chance, with depths under 1 foot in a 1% flood.
  • AE, AH and AO: 1% annual chance zones, with base flood elevations in AE.
  • VE: velocity zone with waves of 3 feet or more.

Anyone can look up a property's zone and find elevation certificates on Forerunner, the city's public tool. Buyers will probably check the same data, and a seller who looked first is never surprised.

Government spending, mostly military, is the largest part of Norfolk's economy. Naval Station Norfolk is the headquarters of U.S. Fleet Forces Command, and the base hosts a NATO command. The Virginia Port Authority is headquartered in the city and operates Norfolk International Terminals, and Sentara Health is also based here.

For sellers, the effect is timing. A household with new orders may need to close in a few weeks, and a landlord whose tenant has a short lease may want out before the next rotation. A cash sale fits those calendars because no loan approval has to come through.

Norfolk runs its tax year from July 1 to June 30 and bills in four payments. The City Assessor sets the value, the City Council sets the rate and the Treasurer collects.

PaymentDue date
First quarterSeptember 30
Second quarterDecember 5
Third quarterMarch 31
Fourth quarterJune 5

The Treasurer bills more than 68,000 taxable parcels and mails bills at least 30 days ahead. Assessment questions go to the City Assessor's Office at 757-664-4732. The Treasurer's Real Estate Tax page also gives tax relief contacts at the Department of Human Services.

The Treasurer also collects nuisance abatement liens sent over by Neighborhood Quality, and owners get 30 days to pay. If the city has ever cleaned up weeds, trash or a structure problem at your house, ask the Treasurer for a payoff before you list or sign a contract.

Unpaid real estate tax can end in a public sale under Virginia Code 58.1-3975, which the Treasurer runs as an online auction of delinquent parcels. Selling first avoids that outcome. Taxes and liens are normally cleared from the proceeds at closing, so owing money does not stop a sale.

sections.h2: Selling for cash, step by step
sections.html:
A cash sale in Norfolk uses the same Virginia deed rules as any other sale. It skips the loan and the repair list.

  • Gather the deed, the latest tax bill and any payoff letters.
  • Check for city liens, including nuisance abatement charges.
  • Look up the flood zone on Forerunner.
  • Choose a settlement company and sign the contract.

After signing, the settlement company searches title, pays off liens and taxes from your proceeds and records the deed. With no underwriter in the picture, the closing day on the contract is the one you get.

sections.h2: Closing costs and the grantor tax
sections.html: On the deed, Virginia charges a grantor tax of 50 cents for each $500 of value. The seller normally pays it unless the contract says otherwise. The deed must show the price on its first page before the clerk will record it. Your settlement agent can give you exact figures for your sale.

sections.h2: What to bring and what to expect
sections.html:
Have the deed, the last tax bill and any loan payoff letters together before you start. If the city has sent notices about your house, bring those too. For a rental, add the lease and the tenant's contact details. For an inherited house, know who has authority to sign and where each heir lives.

You do not need to repair anything. Water damage in a crawl space, old wiring or a worn roof will be reflected in the price, not in a to-do list. Photos of the lowest floor and any flood claim records speed things up.

The problems repeat, and the low, wet location explains many of them.

  • Water damage in crawl spaces, basements and first floors on low lots.
  • Older houses with outdated wiring, plumbing or roofs.
  • Inherited houses with several heirs and no clear next step.
  • Rental properties with tenants, deferred repairs or city notices.
  • Back taxes or city liens that need to be paid at closing.

Buyers who need a loan often ask for repairs, and that can stall a listing. A direct sale lets you pick the closing date and hand over the house as it stands.

faqs.q: Is Norfolk a city or a county?
faqs.a: Norfolk is an independent city. It is not inside a county, so the city handles assessments, tax bills and zoning itself.

faqs.q: When are Norfolk real estate taxes due?
faqs.a: Bills come quarterly, due September 30, December 5, March 31 and June 5. The fiscal year runs July 1 to June 30.

faqs.q: How do I check whether my Norfolk house is in a flood zone?
faqs.a: Use the city's Forerunner site, linked from the Flood Zones page. It shows the zone, flood data and any elevation certificates on file.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Norfolk house with unpaid city liens?
faqs.a: Yes. The liens are normally paid from the sale proceeds at closing. Ask the Treasurer for a payoff on any nuisance abatement charge.

faqs.q: Where can I ask about my Norfolk assessment?
faqs.a: Call the City Assessor's Office at 757-664-4732.
